title: Review: Periodic table structure and blocks; Metallic bonding and comparing structures; Ionic bonding and lattices; Covalent and dative bonding; Lewis structures; Shapes of molecules (VSEPR)
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD01#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD02#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD03#t2 term and clue written for the game; PT01#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD01#N.15, BD02#N.11, BD03#N.5a, BD06#N.13, PT01#N.12a, BD01#N.3a, BD02#N.12a, BD03#N.9a, BD06#N.15, PT01#N.6, BD01#N.14a, BD02#N.2. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cation
items.clue: A positively charged particle formed when a metal atom loses electrons.

items.label: Dative bond
items.clue: Formed when one atom supplies both shared electrons, as when H₂O joins H⁺.

items.label: Expanded octet
items.clue: More than eight outer electrons on a central atom, possible from period 3 on.

items.label: Metalloid
items.clue: Element on the stepped line, such as B, Si or Ge, with in-between properties.

questions.stem: In a kettle's heating element, the hot metal wire is packed in powdered magnesium oxide, MgO, inside a metal tube. MgO is ionic, yet it is used here as an electrical insulator. Why doesn't it conduct?

options.text: MgO contains no ions until it is dissolved or melted.
Its ions are held in fixed positions, and MgO stays solid at the element's temperature.
Its electrons are all shared in covalent bonds, so none are free to move.
Its ions are too highly charged to move, even when MgO is molten.

questions.explanation: Charge flows only if charged particles can move. In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice and there are no free electrons. Strong 2+/2− attractions keep MgO solid to about 2850 °C.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?

options.text: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen
The new bond formed from one electron supplied by nitrogen and one electron supplied by H⁺
All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen

questions.explanation: The new bond is co-ordinate: both electrons from N. Once formed, all four N–H bonds have the same length and strength.

questions.stem: Predict the H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule, H₂O.

options.text: About 104.5°, as lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs do
About 109.5°, as all four electron pairs around O repel one another equally
About 180°, as the two bonding pairs get as far apart as possible
About 90°, as the H atoms are drawn at right angles in its dot-and-cross diagram

questions.explanation: Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, arranged tetrahedrally. The lone pairs repel more, squeezing the angle below 109.5°.

questions.stem: Silicon melts at 1414 °C. Phosphorus (white, P₄) melts at 44 °C. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Phosphorus has weaker metallic bonding, because its atoms are larger than silicon atoms.
Silicon is giant covalent, so covalent bonds break; phosphorus is P₄ molecules held by weak London forces.
Melting phosphorus breaks its P–P covalent bonds, which are much weaker than Si–Si bonds.
Silicon atoms have more electrons than P₄ molecules, so London forces between them are stronger.

questions.explanation: Melting silicon breaks strong Si–Si covalent bonds throughout the lattice. Melting P₄ overcomes only weak forces between molecules; the P–P bonds stay intact.

questions.stem: Beryllium, 1s² 2s², and helium, 1s², both have two electrons in their outer s sub-shell. Why is beryllium placed in group 2, but helium in group 18?

options.text: Beryllium is a solid and helium is a gas, and group 18 holds the gaseous elements.
Beryllium has four electrons and helium two, and the group number counts the total.
Beryllium's 2s² electrons are in a higher shell, so they are inner electrons, not valence electrons.
Beryllium's outer shell, n = 2, is far from full, while helium's n = 1 shell is full with just two.

questions.stem: An atom of element X has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Which ion does X form in its ionic compounds?

options.text: X²⁺
X⁶⁺
X²⁻
X⁶⁻

questions.explanation: Six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). X gains two to reach 3s² 3p⁶: 16 protons, 18 electrons, charge 2−. X is sulfur: S²⁻.

questions.stem: Hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N, has a carbon–nitrogen triple bond. Methylamine, CH₃–NH₂, has a carbon–nitrogen single bond. How does the C≡N bond compare with the C–N bond?

options.text: It is shorter and stronger.
It is longer and stronger.
It is longer and weaker, as six electrons between the nuclei repel each other.
It is the same length and strength, as both bonds join the same two elements.

questions.explanation: Three shared pairs between C and N attract both nuclei more strongly than one pair does, pulling them closer. Shorter and stronger.

questions.stem: In xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄, the xenon atom (eight outer electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the shape of XeF₄?

options.text: Tetrahedral, as only its four bonding pairs repel one another around the Xe atom
Octahedral, as there are six electron pairs around the xenon atom
Square planar, as the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions of an octahedron
See-saw, as the two lone pairs occupy adjacent positions, 90° apart, in an octahedron

questions.explanation: 8 − 4 = 4 non-bonding electrons: two lone pairs. They sit 180° apart, leaving four F in a square plane.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.

questions.stem: Germanium is in period 4, group 14. Which is the full electron configuration of a germanium atom?

options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴

questions.explanation: Period 4, p-block: fill up to 4p. Group 14 gives 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons, 4s² 4p². With the 3d¹⁰, the total is 32 electrons.

questions.stem: Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181. Which shows the strength of the ionic bonding in NaF, NaCl and KCl in decreasing order?

options.text: KCl > NaCl > NaF
NaF > NaCl > KCl
NaF > KCl > NaCl
NaF = NaCl = KCl

questions.explanation: All are 1+ and 1−, so radii decide. Radius sums: NaF 235, NaCl 283, KCl 319 pm. Closer centres, stronger attraction.

questions.stem: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?

options.text: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻

questions.explanation: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both. That attraction is the covalent bond.
